In Defense of the Aimless Afternoon

I want to make a case for the aimless afternoon, the hour that refuses to be useful. Not the rest that prepares you for more work, not the walk taken to close your exercise rings, not the book read so you can say you’ve read it. I mean the kind of time that unspools without a product: sitting on a bench watching pigeons argue over a crust, wandering through a neighborhood without a destination, lying on the floor listening to one song twice because the first time you were thinking about something else. We have become suspicious of such hours. We call them wasted, or feel them as a low-grade guilt, as if the day were a ledger that must balance.

But not every hour owes us an output. Some hours exist only to be lived. I remember an afternoon last autumn when I left my phone at home by accident. At first I felt a small panic, the phantom weight in my pocket. But within twenty minutes the panic turned into something else: an unexpected lightness. I walked slowly, with no map. I noticed the way a barber swept hair into a neat pile outside his shop. I noticed a child on a scooter negotiating a curb with tremendous seriousness. I heard two old men arguing about whether a local restaurant had moved or closed, and I couldn’t look it up, so the argument remained beautifully unresolved. The afternoon asked nothing of me, and I remember it more clearly than whole months of productive days.

We live in an age of optimization. Our steps are counted, our sleep scored, our reading tracked, our leisure photographed. Even relaxation has become a task, something to do well. The language of the workplace has colonized our inner lives: we “invest” in friendships, “process” emotions, “curate” our weekends. There is value in this, of course. Structure can be kind. Metrics can reveal truths. But when every activity must be justified, we lose the quiet skill of doing something for no reason. We lose the ability to be unproductive without apology.

There is a particular kind of attention that only aimlessness allows. When you have no goal, your eyes roam. You see the small, strange details that schedules train you to ignore: the shadow of a fire escape striped across a brick wall, the smell of rain before it arrives, the exact blue of dusk in a suburban sky. This is not daydreaming as escape; it is daydreaming as encounter. The poet Mary Oliver wrote, “Attention is the beginning of devotion.” But attention cannot be forced. It arrives when we stop aiming at something long enough to be surprised.

I think also of childhood boredom. So many of us remember being bored as children, and we remember it fondly, though at the time it felt like a curse. Boredom was the doorway to invention. Out of boredom, we built forts, made up games, drew comics, talked to ourselves, stared at the ceiling until it became a landscape. Boredom was not empty; it was full of possibility. As adults, we rarely allow ourselves to be bored. At the first hint of emptiness, we reach for our phones, filling every crack of silence with news, entertainment, conversation, anything to avoid the feeling of unoccupied time. But in doing so, we also avoid the creativity that needs that emptiness to grow.

There is a French phrase, *flâner*, which means to stroll, to wander, to observe without purpose. The flâneur was a figure of the nineteenth century, a person who walked the city simply to see it. I wonder if we have forgotten how to flâner. Modern cities are designed for efficiency, for getting from A to B quickly. Our phones make sure we never get lost. But getting lost, in the literal and metaphorical sense, is one of the most fertile things a mind can do. When you don’t know exactly where you are, you look more closely. When you don’t know exactly what you think, you listen more carefully.

This is not a new problem. Long before smartphones, thinkers worried about the acceleration of life. Henry David Thoreau went to the woods to live deliberately, not because he hated society but because he wanted to know if he was awake. Blaise Pascal wrote that all of humanity’s problems stem from our inability to sit quietly in a room alone. The attention economy didn’t invent distraction; it simply monetized it. Every notification is a small request for your awareness, and the sheer volume of requests leaves little room for the kind of meandering thought that has no immediate payoff. To protect aimlessness, then, is not to reject technology wholesale. It is to draw a boundary around your attention and say: this hour is not for sale. It is a small act of sovereignty, a refusal to be harvested.

None of this is to romanticize idleness at the expense of action. The world needs people who build, fix, teach, care, organize, resist. Purpose is a gift. But purpose needs a counterweight. A life lived entirely in pursuit of goals becomes brittle. The aimless afternoon softens it. It reminds us that we are not machines, that our value is not measured by our output, that some of the best things—love, wonder, peace—happen when we are not trying to achieve them.

So here is my modest proposal: once in a while, give yourself an hour with no purpose. Don’t document it. Don’t plan it. Don’t turn it into a story for someone else. Walk outside. Sit somewhere. Watch whatever passes. Let your attention drift like a kite with no string. You will likely feel uncomfortable at first, the old guilt rising, the voice that says you should be doing something. Let that voice talk. Then let it go. The afternoon will take care of the rest. You may find that the time you thought was wasted was actually the only time that was fully yours.
